details: A schema makes data predictable for every producer and consumer. When it changes (a new field, a renamed column, a changed unit) the schema version should change too, so old and new data are not silently mixed.
example: Training record schema v3: metadata {impression_id: string, prediction_time: timestamp, …}, features {…}, labels {clicked: int}, sample_weight: float.

definition: A number a model assigns to a candidate for ordering; it may or may not be a calibrated probability.
details: Ranking needs only that better candidates get higher scores. Some scores, such as a calibrated pCTR, can also be read as probabilities; others, such as a dot product from a retrieval model, cannot. Do not multiply a non-probability score by a bid.
example: A two-tower dot product of 4.2 for (U7, A42) means A42 is a closer match than an item with 1.3. It does not mean a 420% click chance.

definition: When the examples you observe differ systematically from the population you care about, because of how they were selected.
details: Recommendation logs only contain outcomes for items the old system chose to show, and post-click data only contains users who clicked. A model trained on such data can be wrong on the population it is actually applied to.
example: A post-click CVR model is trained on the 2% of impressions that were clicked, then applied to all candidates. Those who click may convert at very different rates from everyone else.

definition: A model designed to use the order of events in a history, for example through positions, timestamps, or step-by-step processing.
details: Pooling throws order away; sequence models keep it. Recurrent models process events one by one; other designs add position or time information to each event's embedding and let the model relate events to each other. Order matters when recent behavior or transitions such as 'viewed, then bought' carry signal.
example: A sequence model can tell [shoes, shoes, books] from [books, shoes, shoes]; a mean pool cannot.

definition: Running a trained model on live requests to produce predictions; also called inference.
details: At serving time the system has features but not labels, and it must respond quickly, often within milliseconds. Every feature and preprocessing step used in training must be reproducible here with the same definitions.
example: When U7 opens the home feed, the serving system builds x for each candidate, runs the model, and ranks by pCTR.

definition: The size of an array along each of its dimensions, written like B × 5.
details: Shapes must match what the model expects; mismatches are among the most common errors. Writing shapes down for every input is the quickest way to check a data pipeline.
example: history_item_ids has shape B × 5; with B = 32 that is 32 rows of 5 indices. A click label of shape B × 1 has 32 rows of one value each.

definition: The function σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(−z)), which squashes any real number into a value between 0 and 1.
details: Click models usually end with a raw number z (any value from very negative to very positive) and pass it through a sigmoid to get a probability. z = 0 gives 0.5, large positive z approaches 1, and large negative z approaches 0.

definition: A categorical feature whose conceptual one-hot vector is almost all zeros; the model receives its compact integer index instead.
details: 'Sparse' describes the one-hot representation: with a million possible items, only one slot is 1. Systems never build that vector; they pass the index and look up an embedding. In ads systems, 'sparse features' and 'categorical ID features' usually mean the same thing.
example: candidate_item_id A42 is sparse: conceptually a million-length vector with a single 1, in practice the index 42.

definition: A measure of how spread out values are around their mean, in the same units as the values.
details: Compute the average squared distance from the mean, then take the square root. In standardization, dividing by the standard deviation puts features with different units on a similar scale.
example: Prices $50, $100, $150 have mean $100 and (population) standard deviation ≈ $40.8.

definition: Rescaling a numerical feature as (x − mean) / standard deviation, using statistics fitted on training data.
details: After standardization a feature has mean 0 and standard deviation 1 on the training set, so features in very different units become comparable. The mean and standard deviation must come from training data only and be reused at serving.
example: Training prices have mean $100 and standard deviation $50. A42's $80 becomes (80 − 100)/50 = −0.4.

definition: The product location where items appear, such as the home feed, search results page, or a sidebar placement.
details: Users behave very differently on different surfaces, so surface is usually an important context feature. It also determines the layout, how many slots there are, and what counts as an impression.
example: req_10 came from surface = home_feed, which maps to index 2.

definition: Rules set by an advertiser that limit which users or contexts their ads may be shown to.
details: Targeting decides eligibility before scoring: an ad targeted to mobile users is never a candidate on desktop. This shapes the training data, because each ad's impressions come only from its targeted audience.
example: Ad A42 targets mobile users in a set of countries, so U9 on desktop never sees it as a candidate.

definition: Dividing data by time: train on older events, validate on a later period, and test on a still later one.
details: A temporal split mimics real deployment, where a model trained on the past predicts the future. It catches problems a random split hides, such as new items and changing behavior. It does not by itself prevent leakage from immature labels, which must be checked separately.
example: Train: Nov 1–20. Validation: Nov 21–25. Test: Nov 26–30.

definition: A numerical array with a shape and a data type; the form in which models receive data.
details: A single number is a 0-dimensional tensor, a vector is 1-dimensional, a matrix is 2-dimensional, and so on. Every model input, such as IDs, dense features, histories, masks, and labels, becomes a tensor with an agreed shape and type.
example: history_mask = [[True, True, True, False, False]] is a boolean tensor of shape 1 × 5.

definition: Held-out examples used once, at the end, to report how well the final chosen model performs.
details: The test set is used for neither training nor choosing settings, so its result is an honest estimate. Repeatedly checking the test set while tuning turns it into a second validation set and makes the reported number optimistic. For probability metrics it should reflect real traffic, not be downsampled.
example: After choosing the best model on Nov 21–25 validation data, report its AUC and log loss once on Nov 26–30.

definition: A recorded date and time attached to an event, such as when it occurred or when it became available.
details: Timestamps are what make point-in-time correctness possible. Training rows typically carry several: prediction_time, shown_at, clicked_at, available_at, label_finalized_at. Keep them in one time zone, usually UTC, to avoid off-by-hours bugs.

definition: A small unit of text, such as a word or piece of a word, that a text model processes.
details: Text models first split a string into tokens, map each to an index in a token vocabulary, and look up embeddings, the same pattern as categorical features. An item title can be fed to the recommender as tokens or as a single vector from a text encoder.
example: 'Lightweight running shoe' might become tokens ['Light', 'weight', 'running', 'shoe'].

definition: The process of adjusting a model's parameters so its predictions match labels in historical data.
details: Training repeatedly takes a batch, computes predictions, measures the loss against the labels, and updates parameters by gradient descent. It uses the training split only; the validation and test splits are kept aside to check the result.
example: Each step: prediction = model(x); loss = mean(weight × BCE(prediction, y)); update parameters to reduce loss.

definition: Any difference between how inputs are produced for training and how they are produced live, which makes the live model see unfamiliar data.
details: Skew arises when training and serving use different code, different vocabularies, different scaling statistics, different history rules, or different data sources. The model then receives inputs at serving time that mean something different from what it learned on. Sharing preprocessing code and logging serving features both help.
example: Training divides price by 100, but the serving code passes raw dollars. The model sees 80.0 instead of 0.80 and its predictions become nonsense.

definition: Keeping only part of a list, such as the most recent L events, to bound its length.
details: Histories can be thousands of events long, but models need a fixed maximum. Truncation decides which events survive, usually the most recent. The rule and L must be documented and identical in training and serving.
example: With L = 5 and a history of 8 events, keep the 5 most recent and drop the 3 oldest.

definition: A retrieval model with two separate networks: one turns the user and context into a vector, the other turns an item into a vector; their dot product is the match score.
details: Because the towers are separate, item vectors can be computed in advance for the whole catalog and searched quickly with a nearest-neighbor index. The cost is that the user and item never interact inside the model, so two-tower models are less precise than full ranking models.
example: User tower(U7, history, mobile) → [0.5, 1.0]; item tower(A42) → [0.2, 0.4]; score = 0.5×0.2 + 1.0×0.4 = 0.5.

definition: Coordinated Universal Time, the worldwide reference time with no daylight saving; a trailing Z on a timestamp means UTC.
details: Storing all log times in UTC avoids confusion across time zones and daylight-saving changes. Local time can still be derived as a feature when daily patterns matter.
example: 2026-11-01T10:00:00Z is 10:00 UTC, which is 18:00 in Singapore (UTC+8).

definition: Held-out examples used to compare models and choose settings before the final test.
details: Training data shows how well the model memorized; validation data shows how well it generalizes. You use it to pick hyperparameters, decide when to stop training, and choose between model versions. Because you make decisions with it, a separate test set is needed for an unbiased final number.
example: Try embedding sizes 16, 32, and 64; pick 32 because it gives the lowest log loss on Nov 21–25 validation data.

definition: An ordered list of numbers, such as an embedding or a row of dense features.
details: The position of each number matters: the second entry always means the same thing across vectors of the same kind. Vectors are combined by concatenation, weighted sums, and dot products.
example: [0.12, −0.40, 0.08, 0.31] is a 4-dimensional vector.

definition: A conversion credited to an impression even though the user never clicked it.
details: Someone may see an ad, not click, and buy later. Some attribution rules credit that impression. Such conversions are not covered by pCTR × post-click pCVR, which only counts click-attributed conversions.
example: U9 sees ad A42 at 20:00 without clicking and buys the shoes the next morning. Under a 1-day view-through rule, that impression gets conversion credit.

definition: The set of known values for a categorical feature together with the mapping from each value to an integer index.
details: A vocabulary is fitted on training data, saved with the model, and reused unchanged at serving. It should include reserved entries for padding and unknown values. Each feature normally has its own vocabulary, though candidate and history item IDs often share one.
example: Category vocabulary: PAD → 0, UNKNOWN → 1, shoes → 2, books → 3, cameras → 4.

definition: How long a user spends viewing an item such as a video; often used as a numerical training target.
details: Clicks can be misleading for video: a clickbait thumbnail gets clicks but short views. Watch time captures engagement after the click. It is a numerical target, often only defined for clicked or started items, so it needs its own validity mask in a multi-task record.
example: U7 opens a video and watches 95 seconds: watch_time = 95, mask = 1. An unclicked impression has mask = 0 for watch time.

definition: A learned number inside a neural network layer that multiplies an input; not the same thing as a sample weight.
details: Layer weights and embeddings are the model's parameters. A sample weight, by contrast, is a per-row number in the data that scales that row's loss. The two share a word but have nothing else in common.
example: A layer computes 0.4 × price_feature + (−1.2) × hour_feature + …; 0.4 and −1.2 are model weights.

definition: Multiply each value (or vector) by its weight and add up the results.
details: Weighted sums appear in layer computations, in attention pooling over histories, and in weighted losses. A plain average is a weighted sum where every weight is 1/n.

definition: A defined time interval, anchored to a specific event, during which an outcome counts toward a label.
details: A window needs four things: the anchor event (impression shown, click time), the length, whether each endpoint is included, and the allowance for late logs before the label is final. Different targets usually have different windows.
example: Click window: starts at shown_at (10:00:00, included), lasts 30 minutes (10:30:00 excluded), plus a 5-minute log allowance, so the label is final at 10:35.
